title: True Liberty and Unvariable Steadfastness
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Meditations by Marcus Aurelius, in the Jeremy Collier translation.
body: To Rusticus I am beholding, that I first entered into the conceit that my life wanted some redress and cure. And then, that I did not fall into the ambition of ordinary sophists, either to write tracts concerning the common theorems, or to exhort men unto virtue and the study of philosophy by public orations; as also that I never by way of ostentation did affect to show myself an active able man, for any kind of bodily exercises. And that I gave over the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of elegant neat language. That I did not use to walk about the house in my long robe, nor to do any such things. Moreover I learned of him to write letters without any affectation, or curiosity; such as that was, which by him was written to my mother from Sinuessa: and to be easy and ready to be reconciled, and well pleased again with them that had offended me, as soon as any of them would be content to seek unto me again. To read with diligence; not to rest satisfied with a light and superficial knowledge, nor quickly to assent to things commonly spoken of: whom also I must thank that ever I lighted upon Epictetus his Hypomnemata, or moral commentaries and common-factions: which also he gave me of his own.

From Apollonius, true liberty, and unvariable steadfastness, and not to regard anything at all, though never so little, but right and reason: and always, whether in the sharpest pains, or after the loss of a child, or in long diseases, to be still the same man; who also was a present and visible example unto me, that it was possible for the same man to be both vehement and remiss: a man not subject to be vexed, and offended with the incapacity of his scholars and auditors in his lectures and expositions; and a true pattern of a man who of all his good gifts and faculties, least esteemed in himself, that his excellent skill and ability to teach and persuade others the common theorems and maxims of the Stoic philosophy. Of him also I learned how to receive favours and kindnesses (as commonly they are accounted:) from friends, so that I might not become obnoxious unto them, for them, nor more yielding upon occasion, than in right I ought; and yet so that I should not pass them neither, as an unsensible and unthankful man.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the author first realize because of Rusticus?
options: That his life needed correction and cure
That he should become a soldier
That he should abandon philosophy
That his family owed him a debt

questions.prompt: Per the passage, from where was the letter Rusticus wrote to the author's mother sent?
options: Sinuessa
Athens
Rome
Alexandria

questions.prompt: According to the passage, whose writings did the author come to value because of Rusticus?
options: Epictetus's
Plato's
Seneca's
Cato's

questions.prompt: Per the passage, through what hardships did Apollonius remain the same man?
options: Sharp pains, the loss of a child, or long diseases
Poverty, exile, and war
Betrayal by friends and public disgrace
Old age and blindness

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Apollonius teach the author to value above all else?
options: Right and reason
Wealth and status
Popularity among students
Physical strength

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author value that Apollonius could be both "vehement and remiss"?
options: It let him hold strong convictions while staying patient with less capable students
It let him win arguments against rival philosophers
It made him popular with the emperor's court
It allowed him to teach two subjects at once

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the author want to avoid becoming "obnoxious" to friends who did him favors?
options: So that accepting kindness wouldn't compromise his independence or fairness
Because he disliked owing anyone money
Because his friends often demanded repayment
Because accepting gifts was against Stoic law

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author highlight Rusticus's habit of writing letters "without any affectation"?
options: It modeled plain, sincere communication instead of showy rhetoric
It saved him time when writing to his mother
It was required by imperial law
It impressed the sophists he studied under

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: The author credits Rusticus and Apollonius with specific lessons in humility, steadiness, and plain communication
The author argues that Rusticus and Apollonius were mistaken in their teachings
The author describes a political rivalry between Rusticus and Apollonius
The author explains why he rejected philosophy entirely

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the author was "easy and ready to be reconciled" with those who had offended him?
options: Willing to forgive and make peace
Quick to seek revenge
Indifferent to being wronged
Unable to forget an insult

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what kind of knowledge did the author learn not to be satisfied with?
options: A light and superficial knowledge
Knowledge gained only from books
Knowledge shared by sophists
Knowledge that contradicted his teachers

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the author give up studying because of Rusticus?
options: Rhetoric and poetry, and elegant neat language
Mathematics and geometry
History and law
Medicine and astronomy

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what example did Apollonius set regarding his own teaching skill?
options: He least esteemed in himself his excellent skill and ability to teach
He boasted constantly of his own teaching ability
He refused to teach anyone he considered incapable
He charged high fees for his lessons

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the author call the kindnesses he received from friends?
options: Favours
Debts
Gifts of state
Tributes

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author mention that he stopped trying to appear an "active able man" in bodily exercises?
options: To show he had learned not to seek attention or show off
Because an injury prevented him from exercising
Because his teachers forbade physical activity
Because he preferred to study indoors

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what the author learned from Apollonius?
options: To hold firmly to reason and stay consistent through hardship while remaining patient with others
To avoid teaching students who struggled
To value wealth over philosophical study
To distrust all forms of kindness from friends

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the author avoided writing with "affectation"?
options: An artificial or exaggerated style meant to impress
Excessive length and detail
Poor grammar and spelling
A tone of anger or complaint
